claims.claim: Tertullian was a Carthaginian Christian theologian and presbyter who lived circa 155–160 to after 220 AD.
He wrote De carne Christi (On the Flesh of Christ) around 203–206 AD.
The work was composed as a polemical refutation of Gnostic docetists such as Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus and Alexander who denied that Christ possessed a real human flesh.
Tertullian addressed the heretical arguments in order to safeguard the Christian belief in the bodily resurrection of the dead.
The controversy centered on whether Christ’s flesh was truly human, because admitting it would imply the possibility of bodily resurrection, which the heretics sought to avoid.
The treatise survives in Latin in the collection of the Ante‑Nicene Fathers (volume III) and has been translated into English, for example by Dr. Holmes.
It is historically significant for articulating an early orthodox Christology that affirms the Incarnation and for introducing the famous maxim “Credo quia absurdum” (I believe because it is absurd).
